analysis.one_liner: Requires federal agencies to get a warrant before obtaining a person's location data.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote: introduced with bipartisan sponsorship in June 2021, it sat in the House Judiciary Committee and its crime subcommittee until the Congress ended in January 2023.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would bar federal agencies from getting a person's location information from phones, apps, or other connected devices without first getting a warrant from a judge. State and local police departments would have to adopt substantially similar warrant rules to keep receiving federal justice-assistance grants. It carves out emergencies involving threats to life and leaves foreign-intelligence surveillance under FISA untouched, and it orders annual audits of compliance.
analysis.who_benefits: Anyone in the United States whose phone or connected device can be tracked, which is nearly everyone: the bill would require a judge-signed warrant before a federal agency could obtain their location history, and would tie federal policing grants to state and local police adopting the same rule.

how_it_helps.text: Each federal agency must implement a policy prohibiting it from obtaining a United States person's geolocation information until a warrant has been issued by a court of competent jurisdiction.

States and local governments that do not adopt a substantially similar policy would become ineligible for Edward Byrne Memorial Justice Assistance Grant and COPS program funds, extending the warrant requirement to most local police.
The Government Accountability Office must study federal, state, and local compliance with the requirements annually, giving the public a record of whether agencies follow the rule.

analysis.who_pays: Federal agencies and state and local police departments that rely on warrantless location tracking would lose that tool, and jurisdictions that refuse the policy would forfeit Byrne and COPS grant money. Private firms selling location data to government would see a main customer channel restricted.

drawbacks.text: The warrant requirement does not apply when the Attorney General or a state's top justice official reasonably believes location data could help address an imminent threat to life or serious bodily harm; in those cases the official must notify a judge only within seven days afterward.
Electronic surveillance conducted under the Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Act is expressly excluded, so the largest federal surveillance authorities remain outside the bill's warrant rule.

Tying Byrne and COPS grant eligibility to the new policy could reduce federal funding for state and local police departments in jurisdictions that do not adopt it, a cost critics of grant conditions would flag.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: A meaningful privacy protection that costs little: warrant requirements before location tracking are a standard judicial check, and the emergency and FISA exceptions answer the strongest law-enforcement objections. The main design question is enforcement, which the bill handles through grant conditions and annual audits rather than penalties.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Judiciary Committee the day it was introduced, moved to its crime subcommittee about five months later, and never received a hearing, markup, or floor vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on June 4, 2021, by Rep. Jaime Herrera Beutler with Reps. Correa, Scanlon, and Spartz, and referred to the House Committee on the Judiciary the same day.
On November 1, 2022, near the end of the two-year Congress, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Crime, Terrorism, and Homeland Security; no further action followed.
The bill attracted five cosponsors (2 Democrats, 3 Republicans) and never advanced to a committee markup or a vote in either chamber.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Federal agencies and police departments that use warrantless location tracking kept their existing practice, since no new rule took effect. Location-data firms that sell to government also kept the status quo.

for.name: Rep. Jaime Herrera Beutler
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on June 4, 2021, and referred it to the Judiciary Committee.

for.name: Reps. Lou Correa, Mary Gay Scanlon, and Victoria Spartz
for.what_they_did: Joined as original cosponsors at introduction: Correa (D-CA) and Scanlon (D-PA) from one party, Spartz (R-IN) from the other.

for.name: Five cosponsors (2 Democrats, 3 Republicans)
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; no cosponsor was added after introduction.

against.name: House Judiciary Committee leadership
against.role: Chair of the committee of referral, 117th Congress
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a markup or hearing on the bill during the two-year Congress; it remained at subcommittee referral until the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: Sponsorship was split across both parties from day one — a Republican sponsor with 2 Democratic and 3 Republican cosponsors — but support stayed small and the bill was never debated or voted on, so no party-line vote ever occurred.

industries.industry: Location data brokers and surveillance technology vendors
industries.note: These firms profit from collecting device location data, a market that includes selling to government agencies. The bill does not ban the data trade itself, but it cuts off warrantless government purchases, removing one of the industry's revenue channels.

industries.industry: State and local police departments relying on Byrne and COPS grants
industries.note: Departments would keep grant money if they adopt the warrant policy, but would forfeit Byrne and COPS funds for years in which they do not, trading a surveillance tool for federal money.
